assets.name: Nikola_Tesla_1921
assets.attire: Dark suit, slightly worn at the elbows. White shirt, loosened collar. No tie at night. Thin, upright bearing despite age. Hair silvering but thick. Working at a desk late at night.
assets.notes: Age 65. Hotel St. Regis period. Working at his desk at 1am. Legs beginning to fail him — moves carefully but maintains patrician bearing. Not frail, not dramatic. Simply old and still.

assets.name: Nikola_Tesla_1943
assets.attire: Black formal suit, increasingly loose on a thin frame. White shirt. Pigeons perched nearby on windowsill.
assets.notes: Age 86-87. Hotel New Yorker period. Final years. Rarely left the room. Fed pigeons by proxy when legs failed. Kept feathers on windowsill.

assets.name: William_Harold_Fitch_1921
assets.physique: American man, mid-30s, clean-shaven, composed expression, economical build. Military posture from his service years. Alert, watchful eyes without apparent emotion.
assets.attire: Hotel night manager uniform: dark jacket with brass buttons, white shirt, thin tie, dark trousers. Name badge. Pocket notebook always visible.
assets.notes: Night manager, Hotel St. Regis, 1921-1923. Kept a personal diary from military habit. Observed Tesla's pigeon arrangement without knowing who the guest was. His diary is the primary fabricated source.

assets.name: Anneliese_Varga_1968
assets.physique: Hungarian-American woman, mid-30s, dark hair cut practically short, wire-rimmed glasses, slight build. Academic bearing — comfortable in field work as in classroom.
assets.attire: 1960s academic fieldwork attire: dark wool skirt, practical blouse, low-heeled shoes. Carrying a leather satchel with notebooks and field measurement equipment.
assets.notes: Assistant professor, Columbia University Department of Animal Behavior, late 1960s. Studied pigeon magnetoreception in NYC. Found the 8Hz geological formation under Bryant Park corridor. Paper rejected without peer review. Left academic research 1970.

assets.name: White_Pigeon_1921
assets.physique: Domestic homing pigeon, Columbia livia. Pure white plumage with light grey tips on the wings — the grey concentrated at the outer primary feathers. Slightly larger than average for the species. Alert, still posture when at rest. Not flighty — arrives with the deliberate composure of an animal that knows exactly where it is.
assets.notes: Tesla's white pigeon. Documented by O'Neill in Prodigal Genius. She arrived from the northeast — from the direction of Bryant Park. Never given a name in this episode. Referred to as 'the white pigeon,' 'she,' and finally 'the signal.' Died approximately 1922.

assets.name: Hotel_St_Regis_1921
assets.notes: Luxury hotel at Fifth Avenue and 55th Street, Manhattan. Tesla's residence approximately 1918-1923. Evicted for non-payment in 1923. Beaux-Arts architecture, opened 1904.

children.name: Tesla_Room_12th_Floor_St_Regis_1921
children.physique: A hotel room that has slowly become a working office. Dark wood desk positioned near the east-facing window — the window always slightly ajar. Papers and calculations stacked in precise arrangement on the desk surface. A brass desk lamp. The smell of old paper and the dry warmth of the steam radiator beneath the window. The window frame shows wear where the latch has been operated many times. On clear nights: the dark mass of Bryant Park visible approximately seven blocks northeast, trees a slightly different quality of darkness than the surrounding buildings.
children.notes: Twelfth floor. Window facing east, angling toward northeast when opened. Tesla asked staff to leave this window unlatched at all hours for the pigeon.

children.name: Hotel_St_Regis_Exterior_1921
children.physique: Beaux-Arts limestone facade at the corner of Fifth Avenue and 55th Street. Ornate carved detailing at the upper floors. Ground-floor awnings over the sidewalk entrance. November night — the air cold, the avenue gas-lit with the early electric street lamps of 1920s Manhattan. A few late automobiles on the avenue. The building rises above the surrounding streetscape.
children.notes: The hotel exterior as seen from Fifth Avenue looking north toward Bryant Park — the bearing the pigeon arrived from.

children.name: Hotel_St_Regis_Night_Manager_Station_1921
children.physique: The hotel lobby desk at 1am: marble counter with brass fixtures, a leather-bound reservation ledger, a telephone switchboard. Dim lobby lighting — the main chandeliers dimmed for night hours. The polished marble floor reflects the low light. A small personal notebook on the edge of the counter where Fitch records his observations.
children.notes: Where Fitch observed the pigeon's arrival patterns across multiple nights. His vantage point for noting the northeast bearing.

assets.name: Hotel_New_Yorker_1940s
assets.notes: Art deco hotel, 43 stories, 34th Street and 8th Avenue. Tesla's final residence approximately 1933-1943. Different geological position from the St. Regis — further west and south, away from the Bryant Park formation.

children.name: Room_3327_New_Yorker_1940
children.physique: Corner room, 33rd floor. Two walls of windows. A windowsill with pigeon feathers — grey-tipped, resting against the glass. Not the white pigeon's feathers: feathers from birds that visited after, that are not her. The desk by the south window covered in papers. Steam radiator. The room of a man who has been in it a very long time and no longer needs it to be anything other than what it is.
children.notes: Tesla lived here until his death January 7, 1943. The pigeon feathers on the windowsill were found after his death.

assets.name: Bryant_Park_1921
assets.notes: Public park in midtown Manhattan, approximately 7 blocks northeast of the Hotel St. Regis. Tesla fed pigeons here regularly. The geological formation that resonates at 8Hz runs beneath Bryant Park. The direction the white pigeon always arrived from.

assets.name: Westinghouse_Pittsburgh_Facility_1920
assets.notes: Westinghouse Electric Corporation research and manufacturing facility, Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. Tesla visited twice in summer 1920, the second time bringing the white pigeon to test whether laboratory instruments could detect what she was receiving.

children.name: Westinghouse_Outer_Office_1920
children.physique: Industrial-era corporate outer office adjacent to the research laboratory floor. High ceilings, industrial windows with wire glass. Heavy wooden desks for administrative staff. Black telephone on each desk. The smell of machine oil and electrical components from the adjacent laboratory. A reception counter. Brass fittings, institutional linoleum floors. Tesla stood here with a covered birdcage while staff measured ambient readings in the adjacent room.
children.notes: Where Tesla brought the pigeon for his 1920 test. Adjacent to the main electromagnetic laboratory where the instruments were housed.

assets.name: Colorado_Springs_Lab_1899
assets.notes: Tesla's experimental station at Colorado Springs, May 1899 to January 1900. Where Tesla measured the Earth's resonant frequency (approximately 8Hz, later named the Schumann resonance). High-altitude desert location chosen for electrical isolation from northeastern infrastructure.

children.name: Colorado_Springs_Exterior_1899
children.physique: A large purpose-built wooden laboratory building on a flat plain at the edge of Colorado Springs. A tall wooden mast rising from the center of the roof, topped with a copper terminal ball. The surrounding prairie is flat and semi-arid — dry grass, scrub, mountain range in the far distance. The altitude is visible in the quality of light — sharp, thin, high-altitude sunlight. Lightning rods along the roofline. The building looks improvised and enormous at once.
children.notes: Where Tesla discovered the Earth's resonant frequency that became the theoretical basis for Wardenclyffe.

assets.name: Wardenclyffe_Tower_1906
assets.notes: Tesla's transmission tower on Long Island, Shoreham, NY. Designed as a global wireless power transmission system. Underground shaft 120 feet deep, with iron pipes pushed approximately 300 feet horizontally from the base into surrounding bedrock. The tower itself was demolished 1917, but the underground system was never excavated. The iron remains in the Long Island bedrock.

children.name: Wardenclyffe_Underground_System_1906
children.physique: A 120-foot deep vertical shaft bored into Long Island bedrock, concrete-lined, with iron pipe branches extending approximately 300 feet horizontally in multiple directions from the base — reaching laterally into the surrounding geological formation. The pipes are solid iron, fitted together in sections, driven into the bedrock by hydraulic pressure. At the base of the shaft: heavy electrical connection hardware linking the underground system to the tower's transmission equipment above. Dark, groundwater-damp, the smell of wet iron and limestone.
children.notes: The underground coupling system that pressed Tesla's transmission into the geological body of Long Island. Not excavated when the tower was demolished. Still in the ground.

assets.name: USGS_Colorado_Springs_Station_1923
assets.notes: United States Geological Survey electromagnetic baseline monitoring station, Colorado Springs. Established partly because of Tesla's 1899-1900 experiments. Operational through 1930s. Logs for 1923 show a directional baseline shift beginning in June, stabilizing by September. Annotator note: 'Shift is directional — not uniform decay.'

children.name: USGS_Station_Interior_1923
children.physique: Small single-story government building, utilitarian construction. Interior: a main observation room with a large workbench holding electromagnetic measurement instruments — analog gauges with needle indicators, brass fittings, coiled copper wire leads. A daily log ledger open on the bench, ruled columns in government-standard format: date, reading, weather, initials. The margin of the August 19th page has a handwritten annotation in darker ink, pen pressure heavier than the observation entries — a supervisor's note added after the fact.
children.notes: Where the baseline electromagnetic shift was documented in summer 1923 — one year after the white pigeon died.

assets.name: Pigeon_Cage_Covered_1920
assets.physique: A small wooden-slatted transport cage for a single bird, approximately 30cm by 20cm by 20cm. Solid wood base, thin wooden slat sides, a simple latch on the door. The whole cage covered with a dark cloth — heavy cotton or wool, dark grey or black. The cloth draped carefully so no gaps exist. A carrying handle on top. Worn at the edges from multiple uses.
assets.notes: The cage Tesla brought to the Westinghouse Pittsburgh facility in 1920. He kept it covered in the outer office while the technicians measured ambient electromagnetic readings. Then uncovered it for 10 minutes and had them measure again.

assets.name: Fitch_Leather_Diary_1921
assets.physique: A personal diary, pocket-sized, bound in dark brown leather that has softened with use. The spine is reinforced with a thin leather strip. Inside: cream-colored pages with light blue ruled lines. The handwriting is in black ink, precise and compressed — the writing of a man who learned penmanship in military service and never lost the discipline. Page edges slightly worn from frequent handling. A cloth ribbon bookmark. The 1921-1922 entries show regular, brief observations in consistent handwriting — the writing of a man taking notes rather than expressing himself.
assets.notes: W.H. Fitch's personal diary. Found in 1989 by his granddaughter in a Queens storage unit. Donated to a neighborhood historical society that dissolved mid-1990s. Partial transcript (7 pages) circulated among local history enthusiasts. Journal's current location unknown.

assets.name: Westinghouse_Letterhead_Letter_1944
assets.physique: A handwritten letter on Westinghouse Electric Corporation letterhead. The letterhead: pre-printed institutional design typical of 1940s corporate correspondence — company name in bold serif type, Pittsburgh PA address. The letter itself written in blue-black ink in a careful but not ornate hand — someone who writes formally for important occasions but does not write professionally. Two pages, both sides of a single sheet. The paper is quality bond, slightly yellowed at the edges. Unsigned. Postmarked Pittsburgh, PA, November 1944.
assets.notes: Unsigned letter received by O'Neill during research for Prodigal Genius. Filed in O'Neill's working papers under 'unsolicited correspondence, 1943-44, not verified.' Not in O'Neill's formal LOC papers — in private collection holding his non-donated working correspondence.

assets.name: USGS_Log_Volume_1923
assets.physique: A standard government-issue observation log, approximately A4 size, hard-bound in dark blue cloth. Inside: pages printed with standard observation tables — ruled columns for date, instrument reading, weather, observer initials. The entries for 1923 are in pencil for the observation values and ink for the initials. The August 19th page has two annotations in the margin: one in darker ink with heavier pen pressure (a supervisor's addition), one in pencil (added still later). The ink on the margin annotations is slightly different from the observation ink — different pen, different hand.
assets.notes: USGS electromagnetic baseline monitoring log, Colorado Springs station, 1923. Observer initials E.B.T. for June-September. Contains the baseline shift documentation and the annotator's note about directional drift. Part of the genuinely dispersed USGS archive — many volumes physically lost during administrative moves.

assets.name: Varga_Research_Draft_1968
assets.physique: A carbon-copy typescript, approximately 22 pages. Standard academic paper format with title page, abstract, numbered sections. The carbon copy has slightly blue-grey text from the carbon paper, readable but not as crisp as the original. The edges show handling wear from the decades in the graduate student's files. Some pages have pencil marginalia — the graduate student's notes from 1967. The title page reads: a study of homing pigeon navigation failure rates in the New York metropolitan area, with geological notes on the midtown Manhattan corridor. Submitted to the Journal of Comparative Physiology, January 1968.
assets.notes: Varga's rejected unpublished paper. Survived because a graduate student she supervised in 1967 kept a carbon copy. Excerpts posted on a pigeon-racing history forum in the early 2000s. Forum defunct; accessible only through archive.org partial crawl.

assets.name: Bryant_Park_Geological_Formation_1921
assets.physique: Not a visible object but a visual representation: a cross-section diagram of the Manhattan bedrock showing the continuous rock formation running northeast from approximately Fifth Avenue at 55th Street, under Bryant Park, continuing toward the East River. The rock is a dark grey schist — the Manhattan schist, the ancient metamorphic rock that underlies midtown Manhattan. The formation shows as a continuous connected geological body. An eight-hertz standing wave pattern (visualized as oscillation lines) propagates through the formation. The connection to the Long Island bedrock is shown at lower left.
assets.notes: The geological corridor the white pigeon navigated along. Resonates at approximately 8Hz — the frequency Tesla transmitted through Wardenclyffe's underground iron pipe system. Varga measured this frequency in 1968.
